lines.speaker: Old Barnaby
lines.text: Ah, hello again! I spent half the night on the hill trying to identify the <color=red>constellations</color>, before realising I'd forgotten the way back.

lines.speaker: Old Barnaby
lines.text: The experience inspired three <color=red>riddles</color> about space. Solve them all, and three new books will be dispatched to the library.

lines.speaker: Old Barnaby
lines.text: I wrote them on a scrap of paper which, by some miracle, I haven't lost. Shall we begin?

lines.speaker: Old Barnaby
lines.text: Riddle 1: I am the star nearest to your home, a vast sphere of burning gas whose <color=red>gravity</color> holds eight planets in their paths. What am I?
lines.hint: Not quite. Which star is closest to Earth and sits at the centre of our solar system?
lines.correctText: Precisely. The sun keeps all eight planets in orbit.

lines.speaker: Old Barnaby
lines.text: Riddle 2: People built me and <color=red>launched</color> me into orbit with no crew aboard. I circle the Earth, beaming down weather images and signals. What am I?
lines.hint: Not quite. Remember: people built it, and nobody travels inside it.
lines.correctText: Exactly. A satellite works quietly with no one aboard.

lines.speaker: Old Barnaby
lines.text: Riddle 3: I am a vast spiral of billions of stars, your sun among them. On a clear, dark night you may glimpse me as a faint, <color=red>luminous</color> band across the sky. What am I?
lines.hint: Not quite. Which of these contains your own sun?
lines.correctText: Well reasoned. The Milky Way is our home galaxy.

lines.speaker: Old Barnaby
lines.text: Three for three. Your reasoning is positively <color=red>astronomical</color>, and three new books are already on their way to the library.

afterLines.speaker: Old Barnaby
afterLines.text: Thank you again. Whenever the sky is clear, I recommend a spot of <color=red>stargazing</color>; just remember the way home, unlike me.
